clues: Found in New Zealand coal seams, it goes by the name ambrite
There are five classes of it, told apart by their chemistry
Because it began soft and sticky, insects and leaves are sometimes caught inside
Admired since Neolithic times, and cut as a gemstone since classical antiquity
Fossilised tree resin, orange to brown, set in beads and rings

explanations: When it occurs in coal seams it is called resinite, and the New Zealand coal-seam kind is called ambrite.
There are five classes of it, defined on the basis of their chemical constituents.
Because it starts as a soft, sticky tree resin, it sometimes holds animal and plant material as inclusions.
It has been appreciated since Neolithic times and worked as a gemstone since classical antiquity.
It is fossilised tree resin, orange, brown and sometimes red, used in jewellery.

sources.excerpt: Amber occurring in coal seams is also called resinite, and the term ambrite is applied to that found specifically within New Zealand coal seams.
There are five classes of amber, defined on the basis of their chemical constituents.
Because it originates as a soft, sticky tree resin, amber sometimes contains animal and plant material as inclusions.
It has been appreciated for its color (orange, brown and, sometimes, red) and natural beauty since the Neolithic times, and worked as a gemstone since classical antiquity.
Amber is used in jewelry and as a healing agent in folk medicine.
